name: Enrichment, Peer Tutoring, and Group Work
title: Enrichment, Peer Tutoring, and Group Work
answer: This idea covers three ways AI can support students beyond remediation: enrichment for advanced learners, peer tutoring, and group projects. AI can help teachers generate and check enrichment tasks, suggest tutoring pairs, and draft group planning materials, while teachers and students keep the thinking and final decisions. It matters because personalization should serve all students, not only those who are behind, and because collaboration can be organized without handing over the learning.

sections.body: The idea is that personalization is not only for students who are behind. Students who are ready for more can use AI to explore topics in greater depth, tackle harder problems, or pursue independent projects. A teacher can generate enrichment tasks and check them for accuracy and challenge. These students also benefit from a hint only approach, since they learn more from struggling with a hard problem than from being handed the answer. The problem it solves is that advanced students can be left with more of the same work instead of meaningful challenge, and that peer tutoring and group work need organization without losing student ownership.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a teacher can create enrichment tasks with AI and then review them for accuracy and challenge before giving them to students. For students who are ready for more, the hint only approach keeps the struggle with hard problems in the student's hands. For peer tutoring, a teacher can use AI features in a spreadsheet to suggest pairings based on skills, then adjust the pairs using what they know about personalities and friendships, and the teacher makes the final pairings. Both the tutor and the student being tutored can learn from the arrangement. For group projects, a teacher can use AI to draft planning templates and role descriptions, while the group does the work and the thinking and AI helps them organize, and the text does not give grade bands, so these practices are described for use across grade levels.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no evidence label for enrichment or peer tutoring, so those parts rest on practice rather than research. For group projects, it cites a review of AI agents in collaborative learning (Ba et al., 2026), which describes tools that help groups plan, divide work, and reflect on how well they worked together. No other study, figure, or finding is provided. The book does not claim a measured effect size or outcome for these practices.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that AI does not replace the teacher's judgment or the students' work. A teacher must check enrichment tasks for accuracy and challenge, and the teacher makes the final peer tutoring pairings after adjusting AI suggestions for personalities and friendships. For group projects, the group does the work and the thinking, with AI only helping them organize. The text does not describe privacy, safety, or legal rules, so those decisions remain with the school and teacher. The decisions that stay with a person include what challenge is appropriate, who works together, and how much help is given.
